title: A close match leads to loss for women’s volleyball - Binghamton University Pipe Dream
content: Binghamton's winning streak comes to an end following three-game run. Women’s volleyball faced off against the University of New Hampshire on Sunday afternoon on home territory. Going the full five sets, the Bearcats fought hard against the UNH Wildcats in an unexpected defeat. Binghamton made a great effort, putting up 109 points total in comparison to UNH’s 103. However, it was not enough, and although they dominated defensive scores and service stats, both their total attacks and hit percentage fell slightly behind New Hampshire’s. Their first set started rocky with an initial service error, but picked up quickly. The score reached a deficit at 3-6 with a strong performance from the opposing blockers. Still early in the game, the Bearcats picked up the pace and a service error from UNH followed by a service ace from junior outside hitter Briana Binagi evened out the score 8-8. The Wildcats responded in equal force, scoring another four points. Binghamton mirrored this yet again, trailing behind but catching up with a kill from sophomore right side hitter Maya Coblentz-Brown and two service aces from sophomore libero / defensive specialist Eve Roman yet again bringing it to a tie at 13-13. UNH and Binghamton remained neck-and-neck until the score hit 22-21. UNH was composed, but fumbled against Binghamton’s energy and coordination, allowing back-to-back kills from sophomore middle blocker Hannah Olmstead, sophomore middle blocker Francesca Pierdonati and Coblentz-Brown, allowing Binghamton to take the set. The Bearcats started their second set strong, leaving no room for UNH to score. The team racked up six points in their favor with strong showings from junior outside hitter Magi Milicevic and Olmstead to get there, despite UNH taking time to regroup. Strong pushback from UNH allowed them to just barely trail behind until 8-7. Binghamton’s coordination and special efforts from Milicevic and junior setter Regan Kadel pushed the team through to a landslide set win at 25-12. Tensions were high entering the third set. Energy and hopes were high for the Bearcats, fresh off two set wins and a cruise through the second set. But stakes were higher for the Wildcats, their shot at winning the game contingent on taking this set. UNH took the lead right away, 0-3, but Binghamton bounced back with a couple kills from Coblentz-Brown, slowly closing the gap. With both teams having strong presences by the net, the Bearcats managed to power through, reaching five points on each side. The teams continued going shot-for-shot, Binghamton’s score lagging behind, struggling when UNH was able to break through their frontline defenses. The Wildcats faltered in response, and the Bearcats took the lead 9-8 for the first time in the set with a kill from Coblentz-Brown. A kill from Pierdonati tied the score at 14-14, and the Wildcats turned up the intensity in response, blasting forward by five points during a scoreless period for the Bearcats. From 20-15, Binghamton was unable to close the gap, trading blows until UNH won the set 25-21. The comeback from UNH thus drove the game to five sets. The fourth set began roughly for the Bearcats. Although the players’ momentum was slowing down, they kept fighting and brought it back 10-9 through back-to-back blocks from Olmstead and Coblentz-Brown into a kill from Coblentz-Brown and seven points in a row. The margin of difference stayed tight between the teams for the remainder of the set, staying within one from 19-18 through the 20s. Great communication and strong efforts from both sides made it a fight for every point, long volleys leading to unique saves and many tests of teamwork. The aforementioned closeness in score pushed both teams into overdrive, extending the set past 25. Binghamton stayed motivated, pushing the score up first, but UNH inevitably followed. The breaking point was 28-28, where UNH first broke the score and gained the two consecutive points needed to take the set 28-30. The fifth set kicked off with a long fight for the first point, which went to the Wildcats. Milicevic fought back with a kill for the second point, initiating a battle that inched forward through the duration of the last set. Pierdonati showed up and showed out, a kill and service ace keeping Binghamton in the game. A brilliant round of kills from UNH was countered by tactical attacks from Coblentz-Brown and strong support from Kadel and sophomore libero/defensive specialist Celeste Ocampo. Despite that, it was not enough to bring Binghamton back, and UNH took the set 10-15, winning the match. Binghamton will try to restart their win streak against Colgate University on Friday, Oct. 9, in Hamilton, New York, at 6 p.m.

title: UNH students scramble to vote after student ID ban. Town clerk explains law. - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — Massachusetts native Azrael Ross’ plan to vote in New Hampshire for the midterm election Nov. 3 is now up in the air. The University of New Hampshire graduate student now studies and lives in the Granite State. Ross hoped to use her university-issued student identification card in the Nov. 3 election, but she won’t be able to do so after the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent ruling to uphold the state law banning the use of school IDs to obtain a ballot. “I don’t know anything about the Massachusetts midterms right now because I’ve been around people who are from New Hampshire," Ross said in a Monday Oct. 26 interview. "I don’t feel like I have enough time now to go back and vote and participate as I should. It’s tough because I thought I would be guaranteed an ability to vote here." Ross said she has been paying attention to New Hampshire’s races for the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate seats on the ballot, but not those taking place south of the state line. Student IDs were barred at polling places in June, when Republican-backed House Bill 323 was signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte. The law was enforced during New Hampshire’s September primary election, though it was being challenged in a federal lawsuit by the Coalition for Open Democracy, a Concord-based voting rights organization. In early October, federal Judge Joseph Laplante ruled the law could stay in effect, but that New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan should not have outright prohibited student IDs during voter registration. The U.S. Supreme Court overruled Laplante in a Thursday, Oct. 22 decision, less than two weeks before Election Day, arguing “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election,” according to the order. Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenting justice. With the U.S. Supreme Court having spoken, Durham town clerk Rachel Deane stated the general election will proceed similarly to how the state primary ran, though with a larger student turnout expected. “Durham is incredibly focused on making sure that anyone who is truly qualified to vote gets to vote,” she said. Out-of-state students must bring proof of identity, domicile, age and citizenship to the polls in order to vote. An out-of-state driver’s license suffices for the age and identity portion, while a rental or lease agreement or utility bill can be shown to prove domicile in Durham. The New Hampshire secretary of state has posted all the requirements. UNH has also posted voting information for students. Deane noted election officials will accept students who provide electronic proof of domicile by showing their on-campus housing assignment through the University of New Hampshire’s Webcat portal. A U.S. passport or birth certificate is accepted for proof of citizenship. Students without either can fill out a qualified voter affidavit in their place attesting to their citizenship. Volunteers in Durham’s election will be trained for all potential voting scenarios involving students. “We’re prepared to assist any student that has no other form of ID to troubleshoot how they can actually proceed with voting,” Deane said. Durham officials said students can vote with government identification and proof of New Hampshire domicile. But students interviewed at UNH aren’t confident most of their peers will make it to cast ballots. Ross and members of her social work program cohort commented on the high court's decision. “At that point, it’s so complicated to even be able to get to vote, and now they’re taking away your ability to use the student ID,” said Vivian Eisenmann. “It’s so complex to be able to do something that we’ve been told is one of our rights, but they’re making it impossible. They can’t take away the right to vote but they can take away all the accessible options to vote.” “There’s never any situation where we should be reducing people’s accessibility to voting. It should always be about increasing people’s accessibility to voting,” Elle Legard added. The student voter identification issue has been debated and litigated in New Hampshire for years. Durham Town Administrator Todd Selig began his tenure in town in 2001. The “highly politicized” topic was spoken about before he arrived at Town Hall, Selig said. “It’s something that I think, generally speaking, on the Republican side, they want to be more strict in terms of allowing college students to vote in the communities where they’re attending college,” he said. “On the Democratic side, they tend to be more welcoming in making it easier for college students to vote in the community they’re attending college.” Deane, Durham's town clerk, anticipates higher turnout at Oyster River High School for the Nov. 3 midterms than during the November 2024 general election. “It’s so hard to predict because these elections seem to be different every year,” she said. Two years ago, over 8,300 votes were cast, with the town reporting nearly 2,500 same-day voter registrations, according to the town. Legard and fellow UNH graduate student Max Murdach will be offering students free rides to the polls on Election Day. Murdach said he works six jobs on and off in addition to his studies. “I have a very busy schedule but I have the offer out there to people,” Murdach said. During the primary election, Legard estimated she drove about 20 students to Oyster River to vote. The master's student is preparing to encounter students who hoped to vote but may not have the necessary identification. “Why are we limiting students’ access to influencing policies that dictate how we live and exist in this community? It’s just wild,” she said.

Coverage from XTB market commentary noted that the shares gained after the numbers appeared. Behind the headline, though, the report showed a business that is smaller in membership and revenue terms than a year ago, which is why the quarter is being read as a repair story and not a simple growth story. This article walks through what the filing shows, how the insurance and Optum units each contributed, what the balance sheet and cash flow looked like, and which uncertainties remain as the company heads toward year-end. The report was issued weeks before today's date, and it remains the most recent full set of results from the company. UnitedHealth Group released quarterly results in October and furnished the full earnings release to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Revenue came, a touch below the reported in the same quarter of last year. Over the first months of the year, revenue totaled. Earnings from operations climbed from a year earlier. The company's chief executive, Stephen Hemsley, said in the release that the quarter reflected discipline and execution across the organization. That is a management characterization, and the filing's tables remain the better guide to what actually changed. The medical care ratio, which measures the share of premium revenue spent on patient care, improved in the same quarter last year. For an insurer, a movement of that size is large, because each percentage point on a premium base of this scale represents a very large amount of money. The release states that the ratio included favorable development of prior-period reserves. That detail matters for interpretation. Favorable reserve development means that medical costs for earlier periods turned out lower than the company had estimated, and the benefit is booked in the current quarter. It is real accounting earnings, but it is not a measure of how current-period claims are trending. The operating cost ratio also improved, indicating that administrative spending fell relative to revenue. Together, the ratios explain most of the jump in operating earnings. Market participants typically watch the medical care ratio because insurers set premiums months in advance and then absorb whatever utilization arrives. Elevated use of outpatient procedures, specialty drugs and behavioral health services pressured the industry in recent periods, so a lower ratio is read as evidence that repricing and benefit changes are working. Whether the pace of improvement can continue without the reserve benefit is a question the company did not fully answer in the release. In the release, the company lifted its full-year guidance for this year. The phrase at least signals a floor set by management, not a ceiling, and it is guidance and not a reported result. That arithmetic reflects normal seasonality in insurance, where medical costs generally rise late in the year as members reach deductibles, and it also reflects the non-recurring nature of some quarter benefits. The change in guidance came with a set of operating commitments laid out in the same document. The company said it is aiming to eliminate of its current prior authorization volume by the end of this year, and that it will pass through manufacturer drug rebate discounts to clients in full by the start of in earlier years. It also said earnings on individual Affordable Care Act plans would be eliminated and rebated members this year. Those commitments are best read as part of a broader effort to respond to public and political scrutiny of the insurer. They carry costs and may reduce certain revenue streams, and the company has not detailed every financial effect. UnitedHealthcare, the insurance arm, reported revenue, down, while earnings from operations rose. Medical membership ended September, compared with in June and a year earlier. Commercial plans covered people, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, and Medicare Supplement. The filing states that Medicare Advantage enrollment has fallen people since the end of last year. In the quarter alone, the employer and individual business lost people and the community and state business lost. Shrinking enrollment is partly a choice. Insurers across the industry have exited counties, trimmed benefits and raised prices in loss-making plans in order to restore margins, and the resulting loss of members is the cost of that repair. The open question is how much of the loss is intended pruning and how much reflects customers moving to competitors, and the release does not quantify that split. Optum, the health services group, reported revenue versus a year earlier, with earnings from operations versus. Optum Health, which operates care delivery and value-based care arrangements, posted revenue, down, but earnings from operations rose from only a year earlier. That swing is among the most notable lines in the report, since Optum Health was a source of pressure when the company reset its expectations earlier. Optum Insight, the data and technology unit, generated revenue, up, with earnings from operations and a margin. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit business, had revenue and earnings from operations. Detail stands out in the pharmacy unit. Adjusted prescriptions fell, which the company tied to membership declines at UnitedHealthcare and at other customers. Lower volume in the pharmacy business is the mirror image of lower insurance membership. Cash generation was solid in the quarter. Cash conversion net earnings is generally read as a sign that reported earnings are backed by actual cash. The debt-to-capital ratio edged up at the end of the quarter. The company said it is aiming to bring that ratio by year-end, which implies that debt reduction is a stated priority for the coming months. Capital was also distributed to stock owners through channels. Year to date, the company spent on its share retirement program and on dividends, according to the release. For a company of this size, those amounts are meaningful, although they compete with the stated goal of lowering leverage. The combination of rising leverage, a large dividend, and an active share retirement program is worth watching. If medical costs surprise to the upside, the cushion provided by cash flow would be tested first, and the company would have to balance its commitments against the ratio goal it has publicly set. XTB market commentary published in October reported that UnitedHealth Group shares gained after the stronger-than-expected earnings and the higher guidance. Pulse Two, a financial news site, similarly highlighted the guidance raise and the operating earnings. The reaction fits a pattern seen in large managed care names during this reporting season, when results that show falling medical cost ratios tend to be rewarded. Still, a gain in a stock of this size can be a move worth many in market capitalization, so it should not be dismissed as small. Price moves after earnings reflect many factors, including what Wall Street research desks had assumed beforehand, the tone of the management call, and positioning ahead of the report. None of those can be separated cleanly from the published figures, and the stock's path since the report depends on factors beyond the quarter itself. The latest report is evidence of stabilization, not proof that the volatility is behind the company. First, the reserve development benefit flattered the medical care ratio, and the underlying trend may be less favorable. Second, membership is shrinking in the segments that provide the largest premium base, and a smaller base can limit revenue growth next year. Medicare Advantage payment rates, member-scoring methods and audit activity are set or enforced by federal agencies, and the company has repeatedly said that such decisions affect its plan design. Medicaid redeterminations and state budget pressures add another layer of unpredictability for the community and state business. These moves could improve trust among patients, doctors and lawmakers, but they may also trim margins. Finally, the pharmacy benefit business operates under regulatory and legislative scrutiny over how rebates and fees are structured. The company's pledge to pass through all manufacturer rebate discounts by the start of in earlier years is a response to that scrutiny, and its financial effect will only become clear as the transition proceeds. Managed care companies have spent the past years working through higher utilization, tighter government payment, and rising specialty drug costs. UnitedHealth Group's quarter fits into that shared story but also stands apart in scale, because it combines the nation's largest commercial and Medicare Advantage insurance book with a very large physician, data and pharmacy services arm. That structure has advantages and complications. Optum's services provide diversification and data that can help manage costs, but they also create conflict-of-interest questions that lawmakers and regulators have raised. Competitors with narrower insurance-only models face fewer of those questions, while lacking the same breadth. In the quarter, the company's medical care ratio and operating margin at UnitedHealthcare show recovery, but both are still modest by the standards of the company's history before the recent stress. Peers reporting this season have also described a mix of stabilizing costs and ongoing caution, and readers should check each company's own filing for exact figures. Sector context matters because the healthcare industry is exposed to the same federal decisions. A change in Medicare payment rules or drug pricing law would not affect insurer in isolation, and results across the group can move together on such news.
